questions.solutionHtml:
onate concentration is a calculated value in arterial blood gas analysis, derived using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation based on measured PCO₂ and pH values.

The equation demonstrates how bicarbonate is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, which then dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate:

PCO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

Understanding bicarbonate levels is crucial for assessing acid-base disorders:

  • Elevated HCO₃⁻ occurs in metabolic alkalosis or as compensation in respiratory acidosis
  • Decreased HCO₃⁻ occurs in metabolic acidosis or as compensation in respiratory alkalosis

ABG components include the following:

  • pH = measured acid-base balance of the blood
  • PaO2 = measured the partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
  • PaCO2 = measured the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood
  • HCO3 = calculated concentration of bicarbonate in arterial blood
  • Base excess/deficit = calculated relative excess or deficit of base in arterial blood
  • SaO2 = calculated arterial oxygen saturation (unless a co-oximetry is obtained, in which case it is measured)

 

pH (Option A) is directly measured in blood gas analysis using ion-selective electrodes that determine hydrogen ion concentration. It is not a calculated value but rather a primary measurement.

PO₂ (Option B) is directly measured using electrodes that detect oxygen partial pressure in the blood sample.

PCO₂ (Option C) is also directly measured, typically using a PCO₂ electrode that measures carbon dioxide partial pressure. Like pH and PO₂, it is a measured rather than calculated value.

Explanation:

Celiac Disease (also referred to as Gluten-sensitive Enteropathy or Celiac Sprue) is associated with Dermatitis herpetiformis.

 

Celiac Disease

Definition

Autoimmune disorder triggered by ingesting gluten-containing foods in genetically susceptible individuals.

It is influenced by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8.

Pathogenesis

Clinical features

Adults:

  • Commonly between the ages of 30 and 60.
  • More frequent in females
  • Silent celiac disease (positive serology and villous atrophy without symptoms)
  • Latent celiac disease (positive serology is not accompanied by villous atrophy)
  • It may be associated with chronic diarrhoea, bloating, chronic fatigue, or asymptomatic.
  • Anaemia (iron and vitamin malabsorption).
  • Dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy, blistering skin lesion) might be present. (Option C)

 

Pediatric cases:

  • Both sexes were affected equally.
  • It may present with malabsorption.
  • Begins after the introduction of gluten to the diet (6-24 months of age)
  • Manifestations include irritability, abdominal distention, anorexia, chronic diarrhoea, failure to thrive, weight loss, or muscle wasting.
  • It may also present as abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, bloating, or constipation.
  • Extraintestinal complaints include arthritis or joint pain, aphthous stomatitis, iron deficiency anaemia, delayed puberty, and short stature.

Serum markers
  • IgA antibodies against tissue transglutaminase (tTG): Most sensitive.
  • Anti-endomysial antibodies (EMA): Most specific.
  • IgG antibodies against gliadin (a component of gluten).

Histology

Biopsy of the second part of the duodenum or proximal jejunum:

  • Increased intraepithelial CD8+ T lymphocytes (intraepithelial lymphocytosis).
  • Crypt hyperplasia (Increased mitosis).
  • Villous atrophy (Reduced mucosal surface area, causing malabsorption).
  • Inflammatory cell infiltration.

Ulcerative colitis (Option A) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that affects the colon and rectum. It causes ulceration and inflammation of the inner lining of the colon, leading to symptoms like bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, cramping, and weight loss. The condition is characterised by periods of flare-ups and remissions and is believed to have an autoimmune origin.

Whipple’s disease (Option B) is a rare bacterial infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei. It primarily affects the small intestine, causing malabsorption, diarrhoea, and weight loss, and can also involve the joints, heart, nervous system, and lungs. It is characterised by PAS-positive macrophages in tissue samples.


Crohn’s disease (Option D) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract, causing symptoms like abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and weight loss. It involves transmural inflammation and skip lesions. The exact cause is unknown, but it’s linked to an autoimmune response.

questions.stemHtml: Which among the following is associated with Cryoglobulinemia?
questions.solution: p>Hepatitis C infection is associated with Cryoglobulinemia . Cryoglobulinemia : Cryoglobulins are proteins that precipitate from serum or plasma at low temperatures (<37°C). They can be a mixture of immunoglobulin and complement components or immunoglobulins alone. They deposit in medium and large-sized blood vessels throughout the body, causing endothelial injury and end-organ damage known as cryoglobulinemia. It is often associated with Hepatitis C virus infection Hepatitis B virus infection HIV Autoimmune diseases ( mainly SLE and Sjogren’s syndrome) Lymphoproliferative disorders. Ovarian cancer (Option B) is a type of cancer that begins in the ovaries (female reproductive organs). It often goes undiagnosed in the early stages due to vague symptoms like abdominal bloating, pelvic pain, and early satiety. Risk factors include age, family history, and genetic mutations (such as BRCA1 and BRCA2). Diabetes (Option C) is a chronic condition where the body can't properly regulate blood sugar. Type 1 is insulin deficiency due to an autoimmune response, while Type 2 is caused by insulin resistance, often linked to obesity. Symptoms include thirst, frequent urination, and fatigue. Treatment involves lifestyle changes and medication, with long-term risks to organs like the heart and kidneys. Leukaemia (Option D) is a type of cancer that affects the blood and bone marrow, leading to the abnormal production of white blood cells. It is classified into acute and chronic forms, with acute leukaemia progressing rapidly and chronic leukaemia developing more slowly. Symptoms include fatigue, fever, frequent infections, easy bruising, and weight loss. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient following a road traffic accident (RTA) with a crush injury presents with crepitus and a reddish-brown wound within 3 days after amputation. What is the most likely condition?
questions.stemHtml: A patient following a road traffic accident (RTA) with a crush injury presents with crepitus and a reddish-brown wound within 3 days after amputation. What is the most likely condition?
questions.solution: lostridium species, typically after traumatic injuries, especially with crush wounds or amputation. It is characterized by crepitus (gas production), reddish-brown discoloration of the wound, and rapid progression within days. Gas Gangrene A rapidly progressive, potentially fatal condition characterized by widespread necrosis of muscles and soft-tissue destruction, often due to late-presenting missile wounds or crushing injuries. Cause Clostridium perfringens Incubation period <24 hours but ranges from 1 hour to 6 weeks Sources and predisposing factors Contaminated soil and feces. Wounds with necrotic or foreign material. Crush wounds, road traffic accidents, amputations. Anaerobic environments in the wound. Common sites of infection Adductor region of the lower limb and buttocks. Subscapular region in the upper limb. Clinical features Severe pain with limb swelling rapidly increases in severity. Serosanguineous discharge. Skin turns brown to blue-black with hemorrhagic bullae. Sweet, sticky odor & Soft-tissue crepitus. Complication Septicaemia, toxemia, renal failure, liver failure. Circulatory failure, DIC, secondary infections. Death occurs in critically ill patients. Investigation X-ray: Gas in soft tissues. Gram stain & blood culture: Large Gram-positive bacilli without neutrophils. Biochemical profile: Metabolic acidosis, renal failure. Peripheral blood smear: Haemolysis. CT scan for chest or abdominal wounds. Treatment High-dose intravenous penicillin and clindamycin, along with 3rd generation cephalosporins, are given intravenously. Polyvalent antiserums given intravenously. All dead tissues are excised, and debridement is performed until healthy tissue bleeds. Amputation done in severe cases Hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Prevention Proper debridement of devitalized crushed wounds. Devitalized wounds should not be sutured. Adequate cleaning of wounds with H₂O₂ and normal saline. Penicillin - As a prophylactic antibiotic. Image {{caption_text}} Incorrect Options: Impetigo (Option B) is a superficial skin infection caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus bacteria, presenting as honey-colored crusts, but does not typically cause crepitus or involve deep tissue. Tetanus (Option C) results from infection with Clostridium tetani , leading to muscle stiffness and spasms. While it follows a traumatic injury, it doesn’t typically present with crepitus or reddish-brown wound discoloration. lostridium species, typically after traumatic injuries, especially with crush wounds or amputation. It is characterized by crepitus (gas production), reddish-brown discoloration of the wound, and rapid progression within days.

Gas Gangrene

A rapidly progressive, potentially fatal condition characterized by widespread necrosis of muscles and soft-tissue destruction, often due to late-presenting missile wounds or crushing injuries.

Cause

Clostridium perfringens

Incubation period

<24 hours but ranges from 1 hour to 6 weeks

Sources and predisposing factors
  • Contaminated soil and feces.
  • Wounds with necrotic or foreign material.
  • Crush wounds, road traffic accidents, amputations.
  • Anaerobic environments in the wound.

Common sites of infection
  • Adductor region of the lower limb and buttocks.
  • Subscapular region in the upper limb.

Clinical features
  • Severe pain with limb swelling rapidly increases in severity.
  • Serosanguineous discharge.
  • Skin turns brown to blue-black with hemorrhagic bullae.
  • Sweet, sticky odor & Soft-tissue crepitus.

Complication

  • Septicaemia, toxemia, renal failure, liver failure.
  • Circulatory failure, DIC, secondary infections.
  • Death occurs in critically ill patients.

Investigation

  • X-ray: Gas in soft tissues.
  • Gram stain & blood culture: Large Gram-positive bacilli without neutrophils.
  • Biochemical profile: Metabolic acidosis, renal failure.
  • Peripheral blood smear: Haemolysis.
  • CT scan for chest or abdominal wounds.

Treatment

  • High-dose intravenous penicillin and clindamycin, along with 3rd generation cephalosporins, are given intravenously.
  • Polyvalent antiserums given intravenously.
  • All dead tissues are excised, and debridement is performed until healthy tissue bleeds.
  • Amputation done in severe cases
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy.

Prevention

  • Proper debridement of devitalized crushed wounds.
  • Devitalized wounds should not be sutured.
  • Adequate cleaning of wounds with H₂O₂ and normal saline.
  • Penicillin - As a prophylactic antibiotic.

Image

Impetigo (Option B) is a superficial skin infection caused by Streptococcus or Staphylococcus bacteria, presenting as honey-colored crusts, but does not typically cause crepitus or involve deep tissue.

Tetanus (Option C) results from infection with Clostridium tetani, leading to muscle stiffness and spasms. While it follows a traumatic injury, it doesn’t typically present with crepitus or reddish-brown wound discoloration.

Cellulitis (Option D) is a bacterial skin infection that causes redness, swelling, and warmth, but it does not produce crepitus or reddish-brown wounds and typically develops over a longer period.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells are located in the centre of the lumen in a venule?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following cells are located in the centre of the lumen in a venule?
questions.solution: n: Red blood cells (RBCs) are located in the centre of the lumen in a venule. In venules with normal blood flow, red blood cells remain in the central axial column , while leukocytes are displaced toward the vessel wall . They are responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and returning carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs. Lymphocytes (Option A) are white blood cells essential for immunity, comprising B cells (antibody production), T cells (immune regulation), and Natural Killer cells (targeting infected or cancerous cells). They originate in the bone marrow, circulate in the blood and lymph, and typically adhere to the endothelium of blood vessels rather than residing within the venous lumen. Neutrophils (Option C) are white blood cells essential for bacterial defence . Produced in the bone marrow , they rapidly migrate to infection sites and eliminate pathogens via phagocytosis . During inflammation , like lymphocytes , they tend to localize near vessel walls rather than the lumen. Platelets (Option D) are small cell fragments produced in the bone marrow that play a key role in blood clotting. They aggregate at injury sites to form clots and stop bleeding, typically found near vessel walls rather than in the centre of the lumen. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Arrange the stages of wound healing in the correct sequence:
questions.stemHtml: Arrange the stages of wound healing in the correct sequence:
questions.solution: 014337dcf">healing occurs in four stages : hemostasis , inflammation , proliferation , and remodeling . Hemostasis: Occurs immediately after injury: vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation, and clot formation. Platelets release growth factors (e.g., TGF-β , PDGF , VEGF ) that promote matrix deposition, chemotaxis, and angiogenesis. Coagulation cascade leads to thrombin formation, stabilizing the platelet plug. Inflammation: Early Phase (Days 1-2): Neutrophils clear debris and fight infection. Vasoactive amines increase vascular permeability. Late Phase (Days 2-3): Macrophages debride the wound, release growth factors, and promote fibroblast and angiogenesis. Cardinal signs: rubor (redness), tumor (swelling), calor (heat), dolor (pain). Proliferation: Days 3-14: Fibroblasts produce collagen and extracellular matrix. Granulation tissue forms, and angiogenesis occurs. Myofibroblasts help contract the wound and bring edges together. Remodelling: Weeks to months: Type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I collagen . The wound reaches about 80% of normal skin strength by 12 weeks and continues to mature for up to a year. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Inflammation:
    • Early Phase (Days 1-2): Neutrophils clear debris and fight infection. Vasoactive amines increase vascular permeability.

questions.solution: > Explanation: Serosanguinous drainage from the wound is considered a "sure sign" of abdominal wound dehiscence in a post-operative hypotensive patient (Salmon fluid sign) Wound dehiscence is the disruption of any or all layers of a wound. It occurs in up to 3% of abdominal wounds and is associated with an increased risk of postoperative mortality. Timing and Presentation: Wound dehiscence typically occurs 5 to 8 days postoperatively when the strength of the wound is at its weakest. It often presents with serosanguinous discharge and may be preceded by a popping sensation felt by the patient, particularly during activities like straining or coughing. The dehiscence may also indicate an underlying abscess. Risk factors: Poor wound closure or closure under tension Infection , hematoma , or seroma at the wound site Increased intra-abdominal pressure , e.g., in postoperative patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or excessive coughing Malnourishment Diabetes Obesity Renal failure Jaundice Sepsis Cancer Steroid use Emergency surgery Management: Full-thickness dehiscence generally requires the patient to return to the operating room for resuturing. questions.answerText: Wide local excision with frozen section
questions.solution: p> Explanation: Wide local excision with frozen section is the treatment of choice for early-stage squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip in patients with no lymph node involvement. This technique ensures that the excision margins are clear in real-time, reducing the risk of recurrence. Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): SCC is a malignant tumor of keratinising cells in the epidermis, commonly arising from the stratum basalis. It is the second most common skin cancer, more prevalent in fair-skinned individuals with chronic sun exposure. Risk factors: UV radiation , chronic inflammation, immunosuppression , chemical carcinogens (e.g., arsenic), and HPV infection (types 5 and 16). Tobacco use doubles the risk. Precursor lesions: Actinic Keratosis (AK) : Dysplastic lesions from sun damage; 20% progress to SCC. Keratin Horns : Raised keratinous surface from AK, 10% may have underlying SCC. Keratoacanthomas : Rapidly growing, nodular tumors that resemble SCC and should be excised. Clinical features: SCC presents as nodular, verrucous, or ulcerating lesions with an everted edge and surrounding induration. Differential diagnosis : AK, BCC, pyoderma gangrenosum, and warts. Microscopic features: Irregular squamous epithelium invading the dermis, positive for cytokeratins 1 and 10 . Broders' grading assesses tumor differentiation. Management: The primary treatment for SCC is surgical excision , which provides accurate histological diagnosis and clear margins . The size of the SCC influences the required margin: <2 cm SCC : 4 mm margin >2 cm SCC : 1 cm margin The recurrence rate is approximately 20% . Surgical excision is the only reliable method for ensuring clear margins. Mohs’ micrographic surgery may be indicated for difficult-to-resect tumours or those with recurrent SCC. @Neet_pg_bot

Paget’s disease (osteitis deformans):

  • A non-neoplastic condition that is characterised by abnormal bone remodelling.

Tam O'Shanter sign: The skull's expansion and flattened base create the appearance of the skull tilting over the facial structures (due to the thickening of the frontal bone).

Picture frame vertebra:

The vertebrae appear enlarged and have a thickened cortical bone due to excessive bone remodeling and disorganized osteoblastic activity.

 

Ivory vertebra:

The homogeneous, radiopaque appearance results from increased bone density caused by abnormal osteoblastic activity, leading to excessive bone formation.

="7cd1a840a2169277719756692d362d">radiolabeled form of glucose, known as Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), to assess glucose metabolism.

 

Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron-emission tomography (PET-FDG)

  • Uptake of 18F-FDG (Analogue of endogenous glucose) in large quantities by cancer cells as compared to normal cells

 

Application:

  • Quantification of tumor metabolic activity
  • Diagnosis (lung cancer) and Staging of cancer
  • Assessing distant metastasis
    • More sensitive in primary lung and oesophageal cancer metastatic disease
  • Assessment of response to treatment
    • A decrease in FDG uptake after chemotherapy indicates that the tumor is responding to treatment
  • Routine surveillance following treatment- not commonly preferred.

 

Not useful in the following situations:

  • High Glycolytic Metabolism tissues: Central nervous system tumors.
  • Inflammation vs. Cancer: Both conditions exhibit increased glucose metabolism.
  • Movement disorders
  • Coronary blood flow

 

Warburg Effect

  • Cancer cells prefer glycolysis over oxidative phosphorylation, even in the presence of oxygen.
  • This leads to increased glucose uptake and lactate production, common in many cancers.
  • 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG), a glucose analog used in PET imaging, helps study this effect.

 

Mechanisms of 18F-FDG Accumulation

Mechanism

Description

Aerobic Glycolysis

Cancer cells rely heavily on glycolysis, increasing glucose and 18F-FDG uptake, even with oxygen.

Transport & Trapping

GLUT-1 transporters mediate glucose entry. 18F-FDG is phosphorylated and trapped inside cells.

Tumor Heterogeneity

Differences in tumor subtype, size, and microvasculature affect 18F-FDG uptake.

 

Clinical Implications of 18F-FDG

Implication

Details

Prognostic Indicator

Higher 18F-FDG uptake correlates with worse prognosis (e.g., shorter DFS in invasive ductal carcinoma).

Reverse Warburg Effect

Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) increase glycolysis in tumor cells via metabolic coupling.

Treatment Monitoring

PET imaging tracks changes in 18F-FDG uptake, reflecting therapy responses targeting glycolysis or mitochondria.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with pain, redness, and swelling around his great toe. His serum uric acid level is 9.4 mg/dL. His mother also mentions that he frequently bites his lips and has symptoms of spasticity and dystonia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with pain, redness, and swelling around his great toe. His serum uric acid level is 9.4 mg/dL. His mother also mentions that he frequently bites his lips and has symptoms of spasticity and dystonia. Which enzyme is most likely deficient in this condition?
questions.solution: trong>neurological manifestations including dystonia and spasticity, and self-mutilating behavior such as lip-biting indicate Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder , is caused by a deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), which results in impaired purine metabolism. Pathophysiology: HGPRT deficiency leads to: Accumulation of purine metabolites Excessive uric acid production Neurological complications (dystonia and spasticity) Lesch-Nyhan syndrome Cause Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT) Inheritance X-linked recessive Variants Classic Lesch-Nyhan syndrome : Undetectable HPRT levels. Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome : Partial HPRT deficiency with variable neurological dysfunction. Clinical Features Self-injurious behaviour : Biting lips, fingers, tongue; begins with tooth eruption. Cognitive impairment : Intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe. Movement disorder : Starts with hypotonia, progresses to dystonia, choreoathetosis, oromandibular dystonia, and inspiratory stridor. Oculomotor apraxia : Difficulty controlling eye movements. Dysarthric speech : Difficulty speaking clearly. Complications Hyperuricemia : Causes gout and kidney stones. Neurological symptoms : Abnormalities in the dopamine system, reduced dopamine transporters. Treatment Allopurinol : Reduces uric acid levels and manages hyperuricemia. Symptom management : Controls movement disorders and self-injurious behaviours. Incorrect Options: Cystathionine beta-synthase (Option A): This enzyme is involved in homocysteine metabolism, and its deficiency would lead to homocystinuria with manifestations like lens dislocation, skeletal abnormalities, and thromboembolism . It does not cause hyperuricemia or self-mutilating behavior. Dihydrothymidine oxidase (Option B): This enzyme is involved in pyrimidine metabolism, and its deficiency would not cause elevated uric acid levels or neurological symptoms seen in this case. Xanthine oxidase (Option D): Deficiency of this enzyme causes xanthinuria, characterized by low uric acid levels, not elevation as seen in this case. Its manifestations include abdominal pain, recurrent UTI, hematuria & muscle cramping. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>neurological manifestations including dystonia and spasticity, and self-mutilating behavior such as lip-biting indicate Lesch-Nyhan syndrome.
  • Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder, is caused by a deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT), which results in impaired purine metabolism.

    • Pathophysiology:

    • HGPRT deficiency leads to:
      • Accumulation of purine metabolites
      • Excessive uric acid production
      • Neurological complications (dystonia and spasticity)

    Lesch-Nyhan syndrome

    Cause

    Deficiency of hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HPRT)

    Inheritance

    X-linked recessive

    Variants
    • Classic Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: Undetectable HPRT levels.
    • Kelley-Seegmiller syndrome: Partial HPRT deficiency with variable neurological dysfunction.

    Clinical Features
    • Self-injurious behaviour: Biting lips, fingers, tongue; begins with tooth eruption.
    • Cognitive impairment: Intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
    • Movement disorder: Starts with hypotonia, progresses to dystonia, choreoathetosis, oromandibular dystonia, and inspiratory stridor.
    • Oculomotor apraxia: Difficulty controlling eye movements.
    • Dysarthric speech: Difficulty speaking clearly.

    Complications
    • Hyperuricemia: Causes gout and kidney stones.
    • Neurological symptoms: Abnormalities in the dopamine system, reduced dopamine transporters.

    Treatment
    • Allopurinol: Reduces uric acid levels and manages hyperuricemia.
    • Symptom management: Controls movement disorders and self-injurious behaviours.

    Incorrect Options:

    Cystathionine beta-synthase (Option A): This enzyme is involved in homocysteine metabolism, and its deficiency would lead to homocystinuria with manifestations like lens dislocation, skeletal abnormalities, and thromboembolism. It does not cause hyperuricemia or self-mutilating behavior.

    Dihydrothymidine oxidase (Option B): This enzyme is involved in pyrimidine metabolism, and its deficiency would not cause elevated uric acid levels or neurological symptoms seen in this case.

    Xanthine oxidase (Option D): Deficiency of this enzyme causes xanthinuria, characterized by low uric acid levels, not elevation as seen in this case. Its manifestations include abdominal pain, recurrent UTI, hematuria & muscle cramping.

(a branch of the radial nerve)

    Hyperparathyroidism

    Functions of the parathyroid gland
    • Increase the level of calcium in the body (Subperiosteal bone resorption).
    • Decrease the level of phosphorus in the body (Urinary excretion of phosphorus).

    Types

    • Primary hyperparathyroidism (parathyroid adenoma and parathyroid hyperplasia)
    • Secondary hyperparathyroidism

    Radiological features

    • Subperiosteal resorption usually starts in the middle phalanx of the index finger's radial side, leading to a concavity of bone (the earliest bone change).
    • The "salt and pepper" appearance, or pepper pot skull (lytic lesions in the skull).
    • Brown tumor or osteitis fibrosa cystica: Cystic lesions resulting from excessive osteoclastic resorption appear as low-density, multiloculated cysts that can cause bone expansion, often accompanied by hemorrhage and granulation tissue (more common in primary hyperparathyroidism).

     

    • Rugger jersey spine: Characterized by alternating black and white striations, with sclerosed white end plates and black vertebral bodies; commonly seen in renal osteodystrophy (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old child immediately cries after breastfeeding, followed by vomiting and diarrhea. Which enzyme deficiency might be responsible?
questions.solution: g>Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) deficiency. The immediate symptoms after breast milk ingestion, including crying, vomiting, and diarrhea, are hallmark features of this condition. Galactosemia Enzyme Deficiency Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) - Classical type Galactokinase - benign disease with only oil drop cataract. Epimerase - SNHL + symptoms of classical type (Low galactose-based diet can be given, which is contraindicated in the classical type) Pathophysiology Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate (toxic causing jaundice, and liver damage) Inability to metabolize galactose from milk Damage to liver, kidney, and brain Clinical Features Hepatic: Jaundice, hepatomegaly GI: Vomiting, diarrhea, failure to thrive CNS: Seizures, intellectual disability Eyes: Oil drop cataracts Increased risk of E. coli sepsis Diagnosis Reducing substance in urine (positive) (Positive Benedict test but negative glucose oxidase test) Direct enzyme (GALT) assay Genetic testing (Perinatal diagnosis is possible) Management Lactose-free diet Breast Milk contraindicated Soy-based or elemental formulas Calcium supplementation Incorrect Options: Aldolase B (Option A): This enzyme deficiency results in hereditary fructose intolerance, causing symptoms after fructose ingestion rather than milk consumption. The presenting symptoms would be triggered by fruits and sweet foods, not breast milk. Phenylalanine Hydroxylase (Option B): Deficiency of this enzyme causes phenylketonuria (PKU), presenting with developmental delay and neurological symptoms rather than acute post-feeding distress. PKU symptoms are not immediately related to breast milk ingestion. Glucocerebrosidase (Option D): This enzyme deficiency leads to Gaucher disease, characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, bone problems, and hematological abnormalities. It does not cause acute gastrointestinal symptoms after milk ingestion. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
g>Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT) deficiency. The immediate symptoms after breast milk ingestion, including crying, vomiting, and diarrhea, are hallmark features of this condition.

Galactosemia

Enzyme Deficiency
  • Galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) - Classical type
  • Galactokinase - benign disease with only oil drop cataract.
  • Epimerase - SNHL + symptoms of classical type

(Low galactose-based diet can be given, which is contraindicated in the classical type)

Pathophysiology
  • Accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate (toxic causing jaundice, and liver damage)
  • Inability to metabolize galactose from milk
  • Damage to liver, kidney, and brain

Clinical Features
  • Hepatic: Jaundice, hepatomegaly
  • GI: Vomiting, diarrhea, failure to thrive
  • CNS: Seizures, intellectual disability
  • Eyes: Oil drop cataracts
  • Increased risk of E. coli sepsis

Diagnosis
  • Reducing substance in urine (positive) (Positive Benedict test but negative glucose oxidase test)
  • Direct enzyme (GALT) assay
  • Genetic testing (Perinatal diagnosis is possible)

Management
  • Lactose-free diet
  • Breast Milk contraindicated
  • Soy-based or elemental formulas
  • Calcium supplementation

Incorrect Options:

Aldolase B (Option A): This enzyme deficiency results in hereditary fructose intolerance, causing symptoms after fructose ingestion rather than milk consumption. The presenting symptoms would be triggered by fruits and sweet foods, not breast milk.

Phenylalanine Hydroxylase (Option B): Deficiency of this enzyme causes phenylketonuria (PKU), presenting with developmental delay and neurological symptoms rather than acute post-feeding distress. PKU symptoms are not immediately related to breast milk ingestion.

Glucocerebrosidase (Option D): This enzyme deficiency leads to Gaucher disease, characterized by hepatosplenomegaly, bone problems, and hematological abnormalities. It does not cause acute gastrointestinal symptoms after milk ingestion.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female who is a known case of sickle cell anaemia was rushed to the emergency department with a complaint of extreme pain in the legs and fingers for the past 4 hours. Further examination revealed pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and investigations showed sickle cells on peripheral blood smear and high bilirubin(indirect). What is the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old female who is a known case of sickle cell anaemia was rushed to the emergency department with a complaint of extreme pain in the legs and fingers for the past 4 hours. Further examination revealed pain and tenderness in the right upper quadrant, and investigations showed sickle cells on peripheral blood smear and high bilirubin(indirect). What is the diagnosis?
questions.solution: , a known case of sickle cell anaemia, presenting with severe leg and finger pain for the past 4 hours, right upper quadrant tenderness, sickle cells on the peripheral blood smear, and elevated indirect bilirubin is likely undergoing a vaso-occlusive crisis (type of sickle cell crisis) , a common complication of Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) . Complications Acute Painful Episodes (Vaso-Occlusive Crisis) Characterised by unprovoked, severe, symmetrical pain often requiring strong opioids The most common acute event in sickle cell disease. Lasting from days to weeks. Sudden death during acute pain episodes can occur, possibly due to arrhythmias or pulmonary embolism. Acute Chest Syndrome: Symptoms include chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia, and pulmonary infiltrates on x-ray. It can be mild in children (e.g., due to viral infections) or severe with multiple lobes affected. Thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and rapid anaemia suggest severe complications like acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and multiorgan failure. Osteonecrosis: Involves the hips bilaterally . Chronic pain can progress to severe disability; MRI detects early stages, while X-rays are less sensitive. Leg ulcer: Ulcers range from small and superficial to deep, covering most of the lower leg. Painful and difficult to treat if recurrent, long-standing and large ulcer. Other Complications: Priapism Stroke and silent infarction Gallstones/Surgery Hepatic disease Nephropathy Lung/pulmonary hypertension Retinopathy Aplastic crisis: Caused by parvovirus B19 infection Multiorgan failure IDA (Iron Deficiency Anemia) (Option A) presents with microcytic hypochromic anaemia, not sickle cells on the smear. , a known case of sickle cell anaemia, presenting with severe leg and finger pain for the past 4 hours, right upper quadrant tenderness, sickle cells on the peripheral blood smear, and elevated indirect bilirubin is likely undergoing a vaso-occlusive crisis (type of sickle cell crisis), a common complication of Sickle Cell Disease (SCD).

Complications

  • Acute Painful Episodes (Vaso-Occlusive Crisis)
    • Characterised by unprovoked, severe, symmetrical pain often requiring strong opioids
    • The most common acute event in sickle cell disease.
    • Lasting from days to weeks.
    • Sudden death during acute pain episodes can occur, possibly due to arrhythmias or pulmonary embolism.

  • Acute Chest Syndrome:
    • Symptoms include chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia, and pulmonary infiltrates on x-ray.
    • It can be mild in children (e.g., due to viral infections) or severe with multiple lobes affected.
    • Thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, and rapid anaemia suggest severe complications like acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and multiorgan failure.
  • Osteonecrosis:
    • Involves the hips bilaterally.
    • Chronic pain can progress to severe disability; MRI detects early stages, while X-rays are less sensitive.
  • Leg ulcer:
    • Ulcers range from small and superficial to deep, covering most of the lower leg.
    • Painful and difficult to treat if recurrent, long-standing and large ulcer.
  • Other Complications:
    • Priapism
    • Stroke and silent infarction
    • Gallstones/Surgery
    • Hepatic disease
    • Nephropathy
    • Lung/pulmonary hypertension
    • Retinopathy
    • Aplastic crisis: Caused by parvovirus B19 infection
    • Multiorgan failure

IDA (Iron Deficiency Anemia) (Option A) presents with microcytic hypochromic anaemia, not sickle cells on the smear. It also lacks acute pain crises and indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

Thalassemia (Option B) causes chronic anaemia with target cells, not acute vaso-occlusive pain. It is also associated with ineffective erythropoiesis rather than hemolysis-induced hyperbilirubinemia.

Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) (Option C) is linked to chronic inflammation and cytokine-mediated iron sequestration, typically presenting with normocytic or microcytic anaemia without acute pain crises or hemolysis.

questions.solution: ations indicate Erythema infectiosum (Fifth disease) , caused by Parvovirus B19 , a single-stranded DNA virus (Parvoviridae family) The disease presents with characteristic features, including low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory symptoms, followed by the distinctive "slapped cheek" appearance of facial erythema that spreads to involve the trunk and extremities in a lacy or reticulated pattern. The progression of symptoms and the age of presentation (5 years) are classic for this self-limiting condition. Erythema Infectiosum (Fifth disease) Causative agent Parvovirus B19 Age group affected 5 to 15 years (70% of cases) Incubation period 4-28 days Transmission Respiratory droplets. Transmission rates among contacts are 15-30%. Clinical features Prodromal phase: Low-grade fever, headache, and mild upper respiratory tract infection symptoms. The characteristic rash in this condition is a "slapped cheek appearance”, presenting as erythematous flushing on the face. The erythematous rash spreads to the trunk and proximal extremities as a lacy or reticulated pattern. {{caption_text}} {{caption_text}} Management Self-limiting disease Hand, foot and mouth disease (Option A): This condition is caused by Coxsackievirus A & Enterovirus71, types of ss-RNA virus from Picronaviridae family, and presents with vesicular lesions primarily on hands, feet, and mouth. The pattern and type of rash are different, and the causative agent is not a DNA virus. Measles (Option B): Caused by a single-stranded RNA virus from Paramyxoviridae family, measles presents with high fever, cough, conjunctivitis, and a rash that begins behind the ears and spreads downward. The characteristic lesion Koplik spots (on buccal mucosa) appear on 1 day before onset of rash and persist for 2-3 days. {{caption_text}} Rubella (Option D): caused by an ss-RNA virus from Togaviridae family, it presents with a fine, pink-red maculopapular rash that follows a descending pattern. Characteristic Forchheimer spots are a fleeting enanthem seen as small petechiae on the soft palate in 20% of patients with rubella. However, the virus type and the characteristic "slapped cheek" appearance are not features of rubella. {{caption_text}} Forchheimer spots @Neet_pg_bot

    • Painless, well-defined, solitary, mobile masses.

questions.stem: A young patient in the first decade of life presents with grade II splenic injury with no active bleeding. What is the management?
questions.stemHtml: A young patient in the first decade of life presents with grade II splenic injury with no active bleeding. What is the management?
questions.solution: ="customMeta" data-dictid="d4ae50897e16927771884b5c46ba7d">grade II splenic injury without active bleeding, the management is generally conservative. This involves admission to the ICU for close monitoring, with repeated clinical assessments and possibly serial imaging to ensure there is no progression of injury or delayed bleeding. The goal is to preserve the spleen, thus avoiding the complications associated with splenectomy, such as OPSI (Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection) American Association for the Surgery of Trauma - AAST Spleen Injury scale Grade I (Minor Injury): Subcapsular hematoma affects less than 10% of the splenic surface area. Capsular tear that is less than 1 cm in depth without active bleeding. Grade II: Subcapsular hematoma involving 10-50% of the splenic surface area. Intraparenchymal hematoma less than 5 cm in diameter. Laceration between 1 and 3 cm in depth that doesn't involve trabecular vessels. Grade III: Subcapsular hematoma covering more than 50% of the splenic surface area or expanding hematoma. Intraparenchymal hematoma greater than 5 cm or expanding. Laceration is more than 3 cm in depth or involves trabecular vessels. Grade IV: Laceration affects segmental or hilar vessels, with evidence of devascularisation involving more than 25% of the spleen. Injury to the splenic parenchyma that results in major blood loss. Any injury in the presence of splenic vascular injury or active bleeding within the splenic capsule Grade V (Severe Injury): Completely shattered spleen. Vascular injury involving the splenic hilum that results in complete devascularization of the spleen. Management: Management of blunt trauma focuses on vigorous resuscitation. For hemodynamically stable patients with minor splenic injuries , non-operative management (NOM) (conservative) is the preferred approach. Splenectomy is recommended for severe injuries where bleeding control is prioritized over spleen preservation. In cases with active bleeding, splenic angiography and embolization can be used to avoid splenectomy, but this should not delay laparotomy in hemodynamically unstable patients. @Neet_pg_bot

    • American Association for the Surgery of Trauma - AAST Spleen Injury scale

    Grade I (Minor Injury):
    • Subcapsular hematoma affects less than 10% of the splenic surface area.
    • Capsular tear that is less than 1 cm in depth without active bleeding.

    Grade II:

     
    • Subcapsular hematoma involving 10-50% of the splenic surface area.
    • Intraparenchymal hematoma less than 5 cm in diameter.
    • Laceration between 1 and 3 cm in depth that doesn't involve trabecular vessels.

    Grade III:

     
    • Subcapsular hematoma covering more than 50% of the splenic surface area or expanding hematoma.
    • Intraparenchymal hematoma greater than 5 cm or expanding.
    • Laceration is more than 3 cm in depth or involves trabecular vessels.

    Grade IV:

     
    • Laceration affects segmental or hilar vessels, with evidence of devascularisation involving more than 25% of the spleen.
    • Injury to the splenic parenchyma that results in major blood loss.

    Grade V (Severe Injury):
    • Completely shattered spleen.
    • Vascular injury involving the splenic hilum that results in complete devascularization of the spleen.

    • For hemodynamically stable patients with minor splenic injuries, non-operative management (NOM) (conservative) is the preferred approach.

questions.stem: A patient reports to the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue. Investigation results indicate a Hb of 5.9, increased RDW and TIBC, and low ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient reports to the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue. Investigation results indicate a Hb of 5.9, increased RDW and TIBC, and low ferritin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: BC, and low ferritin are consistent with a diagnosis of Iron Deficiency Anemia (IDA) . It results in inadequate haemoglobin synthesis. Causes: Dietary lack Impaired absorption Increased requirement Chronic blood loss Pathogenesis: Iron deficiency initially depletes iron stores (low ferritin) while maintaining normal serum iron and transferrin saturation. As depletion progresses, serum iron declines, leading to reduced haemoglobin synthesis. Hypochromic microcytic anaemia develops once iron stores are exhausted, with low serum iron, ferritin, and transferrin saturation, while total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) increases. Clinical features include koilonychia, alopecia, atrophic glossitis, esophageal webs, pica, malabsorption, fatigue, pale skin, shortness of breath, dizziness, headaches, tachycardia, cold extremities, and restless leg syndrome. Histopathology: Bone marrow aspiration: Increased erythroid progenitors and a lack of stainable iron in macrophages, best assessed by Prussian blue staining. Peripheral blood smears: Red cells are small (microcytic) and pale (hypochromic). {{caption_text}} Diagnosis: Iron Study Interpretation in Iron Deficiency Anemia Serum Ferritin Low (< 30 ng/mL) (depleted iron stores). Serum Iron (Fe) Low levels Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC) Increased TIBC (increased capacity of transferrin to bind iron in response to low iron stores). This leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing Clinical Features Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids. Absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body. Periodic contractions with normal amplitude or high amplitude contractions (type I and II achalasia). Barium Swallow (Esophagram) Dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES (Bird beak appearance). {{caption_text}} Endoscopy: Normal mucosa but may show dilated esophagus with possible food debris, It is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia, such as tumors. ustomMeta" data-dictid="192677035a169277718780b4d6dbbb">esophageal sphincter (LES) fails to relax properly, leading to a "bird-beak" appearance on a barium swallow, which is a classic finding in this condition. It causes difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) and often results in a progressive esophageal dilation above the constricted LES.

Achalasia cardia

Definition

It is characterised by the progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the esophageal wall. This leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower esophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing

Clinical Features

 
  • Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids.
  • Regurgitation
  • Halitosis
  • Chest Pain
  • Weight Loss

Investigations:

Esophageal Manometry

Gold Standard: This is the definitive diagnostic test for achalasia. It measures the pressure and pattern of muscle contractions in the esophagus. (Option A)

  • Elevated resting LES pressure (typically > 45 mmHg).
  • Incomplete LES relaxation.
  • Absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body.
  • Periodic contractions with normal amplitude or high amplitude contractions (type I and II achalasia).

Barium Swallow (Esophagram)

Dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES (Bird beak appearance).

Endoscopy:

Normal mucosa but may show dilated esophagus with possible food debris, It is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia, such as tumors.

Distal Esophageal Spasm: This condition presents with characteristic "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow, due to irregular, simultaneous contractions in the distal esophagus.

Jackhammer Esophagus: This condition involves excessive peristalsis with very strong contractions, resulting in a tight, hypercontractile esophagus. It can cause dysphagia but has a different radiographic appearance.

The patient's clinical presentation, including a fluctuant mass, high fever, and localized tenderness, strongly suggests this diagnosis. Breast Abscess Definition Pus-filled cavity within breast tissue. Types Lactational Abscess: Associated with breastfeeding. Non-Lactational Abscess: Occurs in non-lactating women, e.g., periductal mastitis. Causes and Risk Factors Lactation: Incidence: 3% to 20% in lactating mothers. Common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant strains in hospital settings). Entry points: Cracked/retracted nipple, blocked lactiferous ducts. Non-Lactation: Often in nulliparous women or post-lactation. Conditions: Periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, tubercular mastitis. Smoking and diabetes as risk factors. Signs and symptoms Fever, leukocytosis, erythema, pain and tenderness, swelling, malaise, difficulty feeding, enlarged and tender axillary nodes Diagnosis Ultrasonography: Detects cellulitis, liquefaction necrosis. Confirms abscess size, location, and loculation. Treatment Lactational Mastitis: Antibiotics: Anti-staphylococcal (e.g., cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin). Breast emptying: Frequent breastfeeding or pumping. Support: Breast support garment, cold compresses, analgesia. Drainage: Ultrasound-guided preferred over surgical incision. Follow-up: Regular clinical and ultrasonographic reviews, culture-based antibiotic modification. Non-Lactational Mastitis: Broad-spectrum antibiotics for subareolar infections. Needle aspiration for abscess drainage. Major milk duct excision for complications like sepsis or fistula. Incorrect Options: Breast engorgement (Option A) is not associated with a fluctuant mass, high fever, or localized pain. Acute mastitis (Option C) can cause breast pain and swelling, but it typically does not present as a fluctuant mass. Fibroadenoma (Option D) does not present with a fluctuant mass, high fever, or localized pain. @Neet_pg_bot

Breast Abscess

Definition
  • Pus-filled cavity within breast tissue.

Types
  • Lactational Abscess: Associated with breastfeeding.
  • Non-Lactational Abscess: Occurs in non-lactating women, e.g., periductal mastitis.

Causes and Risk Factors
  • Lactation:
    • Incidence: 3% to 20% in lactating mothers.
    • Common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant strains in hospital settings).
    • Entry points: Cracked/retracted nipple, blocked lactiferous ducts.
  • Non-Lactation:
    • Often in nulliparous women or post-lactation.
    • Conditions: Periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, tubercular mastitis.
    • Smoking and diabetes as risk factors.

Signs and symptoms

Fever, leukocytosis, erythema, pain and tenderness, swelling, malaise, difficulty feeding, enlarged and tender axillary nodes

Diagnosis
  • Ultrasonography:
    • Detects cellulitis, liquefaction necrosis.
    • Confirms abscess size, location, and loculation.

Treatment
  • Lactational Mastitis:
    • Antibiotics: Anti-staphylococcal (e.g., cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin).
    • Breast emptying: Frequent breastfeeding or pumping.
    • Support: Breast support garment, cold compresses, analgesia.
    • Drainage: Ultrasound-guided preferred over surgical incision.
    • Follow-up: Regular clinical and ultrasonographic reviews, culture-based antibiotic modification.
  • Non-Lactational Mastitis:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics for subareolar infections.
    • Needle aspiration for abscess drainage.
    • Major milk duct excision for complications like sepsis or fistula.

Incorrect Options:

Breast engorgement (Option A) is not associated with a fluctuant mass, high fever, or localized pain.

Acute mastitis (Option C) can cause breast pain and swelling, but it typically does not present as a fluctuant mass.

Fibroadenoma (Option D) does not present with a fluctuant mass, high fever, or localized pain.

Correct Answer B - Serum ferritin levels

  • The patient's presentation, with a history of piles and a peripheral smear showing anisocytosis, poikilocytosis, and target cells, along with the microcytic nature of the anemia, strongly suggests iron deficiency anemia (IDA) due to chronic blood loss.
  • Serum ferritin is a key marker for diagnosing IDA.
  • In IDA, ferritin levels decrease as iron stores are depleted. Levels below 30 ng/mL are indicative of depleted iron stores.

Investigations for IDA

Iron Study

Interpretation in Iron Deficiency Anemia

Serum Ferritin

Low (< 30 ng/mL) indicates depleted iron stores.

Serum Iron (Fe)

Low levels are seen in iron deficiency anemia.

Total Iron Binding Capacity (TIBC)

Increased TIBC reflects the increased capacity of transferrin to bind iron in response to low iron stores.

Red Cell Distribution Width (RDW)

Increased RDW is often seen in iron deficiency anemia

Confirmatory test

HbA2 levels (Option A) are useful for diagnosing thalassemia. Although target cells can also be seen in thalassemia, the clinical history of piles and the absence of symptoms indicative of thalassemia suggest iron deficiency anemia is the more likely diagnosis

Serum folate levels (Option C): Folate deficiency causes macrocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia. The MCV here is low, making folate levels less relevant.

Serum homocysteine levels (Option D): This would be more relevant for vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which typically causes macrocytic anemia, not microcytic anemia.
